Infrastructure & the drought

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Gripped by drought, it stands to reason that South Africa must treat every drop of water as sacred -- but we expose how water is wasted and lost due to dilapidated infrastructure

Summary:
In KwaZulu-Natal where the drought is pinching especially hard, more than half of water is lost due to burst pipes and leakages, thefts or other unauthorised use.

In Gauteng, we are dangerously close to over-subscribing our available water...and yet we lose around a third through broken infrastructure and leaks.

South Africa is the 30th driest country in the world, and yet we have invested little in expertise and maintenance -- rather settling for crony appointments in municipalities unable to fix the problems.

According to the 2030 Water Resources Group, SA will face a shortfall of 17% between supply and demand by that year. In his 2010 State of the Nation address, President Jacob Zuma committed to halving leaks by 2014. Water leaks are also targeted by the national planning commission, which said fixing them is one of the cheapest and quickest ways of ensuring a water crunch does not happen.

But losses have steadily increased -- the main reasons given by politicians are a lack of skilled staff, ageing infrastructure, a lack of information, and tariffs not reflecting the full costs of delivering water. The situation is the same across the country.

A report by the Water Research Commission two years ago found that on average a third -- roughly 37% of water was lost in municipalities. This was either from leaks, or from people not paying for their water – both are included in "non-revenue water".

So how has the situation changed in the last two years?

Further information:
To take a current snapshot of the problem of drought and broken infrastructure, we fly to some of the worst drought affected parts of the country and see the state of broken, leaking infrastructure that has caused inconvenience, expense and increasingly threatens health.

Gauteng, with its growing population and industry, faces the biggest crunch in the future. It is already using 98% of its allocated water, and relies on Lesotho for a big chunk of the water sitting in the Vaal Dam. The next stage of the Lesotho Highlands Water Scheme only comes online in 2020, and the province will be running on the edge until then.

So we feature the case of Martha Mokate — Meadowlands — an active member of the Soweto Electricity Crisis Committee and Gauteng Water Caucus, Martha plays a strong role in the community and has been fighting for remediation and reparation of the situation in Meadowlands for at least the last ten years. In the Gauteng Water Caucus, they expose the ineffectiveness of municipalities in rectifying infrastructure problems amongst other problems. Martha & neighbours’ houses are regularly flooded (and have been for the last 10 years…they’ve lived there in houses they inherited from their parents in the 1950s) because there are no storm water drains and the pipes that municipal workers come to fix, regularly spring leaks again. Their children’s eyes are affected by the dust from the mine dumps behind their houses. That dust infects their lungs and, in the rainy season, the acid, toxic water flows off those dumps into their houses together with sewage from the overloaded sewer system.

We also look at Villiers/Qalabotja where Pieter vd Westhuizen says an already dire situation with run-down infrastructure has become worse due to drought, which is very visible and severe there — at a meeting of the Committee on MONDAY this week, it was decided to initiate a pro-active action plan, due to the reigning drought conditions, to approach the authorities to help with an increase in suspected water-related health problems probably caused by the very low water levels of the Vaal which is causing an existing water system contaminated by spillages of raw sewage to become more concentrated. They’re asking for an increase in the water flow from the Grootdraai Dam (the transfer scheme that brings water from Lesotho, through the Drakensberg Rain Factory, to the Vaal system)...as this will definitely contribute to a positive effect in the water quality. As Villiers and Qalabotjha are constantly facing interruptions in water supply, certain of the communities gather their water needs directly from the Vaal river…and the local Mafube Mun as are in contempt of four High Court Orders (Civil Actions) since 2004 due to water pollution. Mafube Municipality are often found to be unable to fund chemicals to service their water works, which is having a definite effect on the water quality in this region. Directives were issued by DWA against Mafube Mun in the past under more favourable conditions with less than zero effect and it is a known fact that Mafube Mun is unable to make contributions as far as their water levies are concerned

We put the narratives from various towns together through the eyes of experts who have watched the national picture for a long time -- Paul Fairall form "National Wetlands in Crisis" and the "Jukskei River Catchment Area Management Forum", as well as Afriforum whose members are in fact some of the retired engineers and technicians that could and should maintain the system. We also speak to the Department of Cooperative Governance about efforts in the "Back to Basics" programme to get infrastructure repaired and working in municipalities where capacity has long been eroded.

Press Release:


Parched Water Future
All South Africans should prepare for days when bath water is restricted to a bucketful and queuing for drinking water is a daily norm. So say experts, as the drought exposes the crumbling countrywide network of water infrastructure that brings water to us all. Surprisingly, local governments have not taken up many simple low-cost innovative solutions that some communities have implemented at their own cost, fixing their water supply. Carte Blanche investigates a parched future for South Africa.



Script:


INFRASTRUCTURE & DROUGHT
In the middle of the summer rain season in the Drakensberg the Tugela Falls should be a beautiful plume of white…but this year, it’s hard to even spot the world’s second highest waterfall. Downstream, province after province have been declared disaster areas as rivers and dams fed form the mountains run low.
CLAIRE MAWISA: Is only El Nino to blame for the crippling drought we’ve faced this summer…or is human error, neglect and mismanagement at the heart of water shortages? 
Earlier this year we told the story of adventurer and citizen scientist Franz Fuls who had set out on a source-to-sea exploration of the Vaal River. The writing was on the wall.
FRANZ FULS: There was no water in the area. The farmers in the area already complained in January that it was the lowest that the Vaal river has been in that area up there in 2 decades. We have been in a crisis point for a while now, actually I almost want to say it’s too late. The only thing that can save us now is good rain, and if we look at the weather forecast and El Nino, it’s not coming. Our ignorance is gonna kill us.
South Africa’s future water security is pinned on a second phase big dam in Lesotho that should be built by 2024, and will cost billions of rands. Complex systems of dams, canals and rivers from Lesotho have served water-poor provinces since the late 1990s.
Water Research Commission CEO Dhesigen Naidoo says these big dams may not be enough, considering how we treat the water once it reaches us.
DHESIGEN NAIDOO: It’s not so much the bulk infrastructure, like the dams…the dams are quite solid, it is when you get into the realm of the waste water treatment works, into the realm of the pumping stations that need to convey the water from one place to another – this is where we have to get our maintenance levels much better than they currently are. 
Martha Matthews’s home in Soweto has stood since 1951. Ten years ago a burst underground municipal pipe on their sidewalk turned the yard into a wetland. Recently, the garden wall collapsed in the soggy earth. 
MARTHA MATTHEWS: Johannesburg Water they came, more than ten times, we are trying. We are not sure, but we will fix it.
DHESIGEN NAIDOO: This is not leaks of raw waterthis is the leaks of water that is treated to drinking quality standard that is lost inside the system. 
Carpets and furniture rot. Rising damp chokes their airways. Martha sought help from Gauteng Water Caucus member for the area, Martha Mokate.
MARTHA MOKATE: What damage has that water done underneath? Any day, any time, the house can sink or fall down on them asleep, then the government will say ‘oh we didn’t see this coming’.
Martha Mokate roped in Judith Taylor from Earthily Africa to escalate the case — Judith monitors various sources of water outage in Gauteng.
JUDITH TAYLOR: In Morningside they have now replaced all of the water infrastructure, but only after they had two major pipe explosions which wiped out a house, shot down the hill and took out a Porsche and delivered it into the house, the bottom of the next complex…it’s the same all over – potable water from Joburg’s failing infrastructure.
Fetching water has rarely been a sight associated with middleclass suburbia…
UPS: woman fetching water – HOW OLD ARE YOU MAMA? 67…and you do this every day?
This drought equalises everyone in the face of municipal ineptitude.
The Bateleurs who volunteer pilots and planes to give researchers a bird’s eye view of the country’s eco-challenges took us to Paulpietersburg in northern KwazuluNatal. With a small revenue-base the town has limited resources. 
CLAIRE MAWISA: Municipalities are generally cash-strapped and experts migrate to the cities – so how will the residents who depend on this infrastructure for every drop, survive?
The local dam became too small for the growing community. Pipes were installed too high to reach the water level once it dropped. Since then Thabi Khumalo’s life is upside down.
THABI KHUMALO: It has been a month to two months.
CLAIRE MAWISA: Did they give you a time when it would come back? Did they tell you when it would come back?
THABI KHUMALO: No, they predicted next year in March. 
Knowing that enough clean water is crucial to avoid the outbreak of disease, civil activists Afriforum took matters in hand. Julius Kleynhans is head of environmental affairs. 
JULIAN KLEYNHANS: There’s a lot of boreholes in the area but they’re not refurbished – I think that’s a tendency throughout the country in your rural tows. Our Afriforum branch had to step up there to refurbish that water and give the people drinking water in the township and the town itself.
CLAIRE MAWISA: How does it affect how you go about your life?
THABI KHMALO: A lot, I can say a lot because we have to limit ourselves. Let’s say you need to bath, we are using the dishes, not the bath tap or the shower. 
Before the borehole was fixed, getting water from an older tank proved stressful.
THABI KHUMALO: Everyday when you come from work you need to rush home so you will get there before there is too many people — that side you can wait maybe ten minutes for a bucket to fill up — just imagine if you come with five buckets. An hour to two hours. People were even like fighting sometimes because the queue as too long. 
JULIUS KLEYNHANS: It was about R80,000. Sometimes it’s just taking responsibility and ownership over something. 
Kleynhans oversees a 130 towns in all provinces from where they’ve received complaints – all provinces, except – so far – the Western Cape. Their members seek to work with municipalities to fix problems.  
JULIUS KLEYNHANS: Another problem in Standerton where the town was without water, it cost us 400 bucks to get a plumber to fix the hole in the pipe and the whole town had water again. 
Disaster province Free State: In Bethlehem sewage bypasses treatment works into the river.
In Welkom blood runs with sewage form the plant.
In Dealesville, residents note days when the water is off – the National Water Act says no South African should be without water longer than seven days. 
In Kimberley, Northern Cape, a week-long outage saw the local hospital unable to provide services like dialysis. The town continuously loses 56% of its drinking water. 
Lifelong water activist and consultant Paul Fairall says declining expertise lies at the root.
PAUL FAIRALL: At least 80% of our municipal waste water works, or sewerage farms, are not operating at all or not operating properly. 
CLAIRE MAWISA: 80%?
PAUL FAIRALL: We’ve got a shortage of about 20,000 engineers. Until we address that properly, this country is seriously exposed to illness such as cholera. It’s not a governmental problem; it’s a survival of the species problem.
The Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs can stage cooperative governance rescue missions when local government fails. Themba Fosi heads up the Support Interventions team.
THEMBA FOSI: There is a lack of skills and quality of leadership in the municipalities, corruption – these are things that are real. We have intervened in such municipalities and taken over the management of some of these functions; Madibeng, Oudtshoorn and Umkanyakhude in KZN…and ensure that we second the right skills. 
Municipal Infrastructure Support Agency CEO Dr Sean Phillips says there’d be enough money for maintenance if municipalities improved their revenue collection.
SEAN PHILLIPS: We’re also going to be starting from next financial year to put in place multi-skilled teams of private sector people to assist weaker municipalities. We’ve been engaging with the South African Institute of Civil Engineers…we think that there’s room for municipalities to be more innovative in their recruitment practices, for example, to offer part-time positions to South African engineers.
COGTA says Municipal top management has had a grace period to improve their skills. Now minimum competency requirements are in place – officials who don’t qualify and who don’t do their lawful duty, should be redeployed away from management. 
JULIUS KLEYNHANS: Cooperative governance is really a get-out-of-jail-free card. We haven’t seen a municipal official getting locked up yet and I believe that if we see that happen then you’re going to see a whole change throughout the industry in the country. 
For Fairall the response does not match a growing population that emits 4-billion litres of sewage daily into a dwindling water supply that cannot dilute the pollution. 
PAUL FAIRALL: Take people from the army, you take a battalion from the army, and you send them in under scientific leadership and you fix those waste water works. It’s a crisis – you send in someone that can manage it and fix those wastewater works.
In addition to winning back the 37% water lost to leaks, the Water Research Commission says we must stop flushing away hundreds of litres of drinking water per person per day.
DHESIGEN NAIDOO: If you move from waterborne sewerage into dry sanitation or very low water use sanitation, we have the potential to make 30-40% more water available inside the system today.
DUDZE MKHIZE: There’s a serious crisis; not just of the volumes to supply, but to change the behavior. 
As Randwater General Manager for Operations Duduze Mkhize is best placed to know what the system can handle — they purify drinking water for 12 million people in four provinces.
DUDUZE MKHIZE: We are trying to now build that sense of urgency to the consumers, to help us, because we can build infrastructure like we are putting more infrastructure next year of 200 mega-liters and we’ll be augmenting that with another 600 mega-liters. But if we don’t change their behavior which the municipalities mainly have to drive…you can have phase 2 of Lesotho…if you don’t have that behaviour corrected, they’ll never win and the prices just keep on going up.
DHESIGEN NAIDOO: Our best case scenarios now going into the future regarding climate change is a 2.7-degree rise in temperature. It means that we’re gonna have increased occurrences of heat waves, increased evaporation inside the system and the possibility of decreased sanitation. We are looking at a water future that is much more challenging than the water present. 
FRANZ FULS: If you have a lawn, stop watering it. If you are used to taking baths, share it with your wife, let the kids share…or rather, don’t even bath, take a bowl man – we are getting into crisis. If we don’t start using a bowl to clean ourselves in now, chances a

JULIUS KLEYNHANS: Another problem in Standerton where the town was without water, it cost us 400 bucks to get a plumber to fix the hole in the pipe and the whole town had water again. Disaster province Free State: In Bethlehem sewage bypasses treatment works into the river. In Welkom blood runs with sewage form the plant. In Dealesville, residents note days when the water is off – the National Water Act says no South African should be without water longer than seven days. In Kimberley, Northern Cape, a week-long outage saw the local hospital unable to provide services like dialysis. The town continuously loses 56% of its drinking water. Lifelong water activist and consultant Paul Fairall says declining expertise lies at the root. PAUL FAIRALL: At least 80% of our municipal waste water works, or sewerage farms, are not operating at all or not operating properly. CLAIRE MAWISA: 80%? PAUL FAIRALL: We’ve got a shortage of about 20,000 engineers. Until we address that properly, this country is seriously exposed to illness such as cholera. It’s not a governmental problem; it’s a survival of the species problem. The Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs can stage cooperative governance rescue missions when local government fails. Themba Fosi heads up the Support Interventions team. THEMBA FOSI: There is a lack of skills and quality of leadership in the municipalities, corruption – these are things that are real. We have intervened in such municipalities and taken over the management of some of these functions; Madibeng, Oudtshoorn and Umkanyakhude in KZN…and ensure that we second the right skills. Municipal Infrastructure Support Agency CEO Dr Sean Phillips says there’d be enough money for maintenance if municipalities improved their revenue collection. SEAN PHILLIPS: We’re also going to be starting from next financial year to put in place multi-skilled teams of private sector people to assist weaker municipalities. We’ve been engaging with the South African Institute of Civil Engineers…we think that there’s room for municipalities to be more innovative in their recruitment practices, for example, to offer part-time positions to South African engineers. COGTA says Municipal top management has had a grace period to improve their skills. Now minimum competency requirements are in place – officials who don’t qualify and who don’t do their lawful duty, should be redeployed away from management. JULIUS KLEYNHANS: Cooperative governance is really a get-out-of-jail-free card. We haven’t seen a municipal official getting locked up yet and I believe that if we see that happen then you’re going to see a whole change throughout the industry in the country. For Fairall the response does not match a growing population that emits 4-billion litres of sewage daily into a dwindling water supply that cannot dilute the pollution. PAUL FAIRALL: Take people from the army, you take a battalion from the army, and you send them in under scientific leadership and you fix those waste water works. It’s a crisis – you send in someone that can manage it and fix those wastewater works. In addition to winning back the 37% water lost to leaks, the Water Research Commission says we must stop flushing away hundreds of litres of drinking water per person per day. DHESIGEN NAIDOO: If you move from waterborne sewerage into dry sanitation or very low water use sanitation, we have the potential to make 30-40% more water available inside the system today. DUDZE MKHIZE: There’s a serious crisis; not just of the volumes to supply, but to change the behavior. As Randwater General Manager for Operations Duduze Mkhize is best placed to know what the system can handle — they purify drinking water for 12 million people in four provinces. DUDUZE MKHIZE: We are trying to now build that sense of urgency to the consumers, to help us, because we can build infrastructure like we are putting more infrastructure next year of 200 mega-liters and we’ll be augmenting that with another 600 mega-liters. But if we don’t change their behavior which the municipalities mainly have to drive…you can have phase 2 of Lesotho…if you don’t have that behaviour corrected, they’ll never win and the prices just keep on going up. DHESIGEN NAIDOO: Our best case scenarios now going into the future regarding climate change is a 2.7-degree rise in temperature. It means that we’re gonna have increased occurrences of heat waves, increased evaporation inside the system and the possibility of decreased sanitation. We are looking at a water future that is much more challenging than the water present. FRANZ FULS: If you have a lawn, stop watering it. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Gripped by drought, it stands to reason that South Africa must treat every drop of water as sacred -- but we expose how water is wasted and lost due to dilapidated infrastructure
metadata.Summary: In KwaZulu-Natal where the drought is pinching especially hard, more than half of water is lost due to burst pipes and leakages, thefts or other unauthorised use. In Gauteng, we are dangerously close to over-subscribing our available water...and yet we lose around a third through broken infrastructure and leaks. South Africa is the 30th driest country in the world, and yet we have invested little in expertise and maintenance -- rather settling for crony appointments in municipalities unable to fix the problems. According to the 2030 Water Resources Group, SA will face a shortfall of 17% between supply and demand by that year. In his 2010 State of the Nation address, President Jacob Zuma committed to halving leaks by 2014. Water leaks are also targeted by the national planning commission, which said fixing them is one of the cheapest and quickest ways of ensuring a water crunch does not happen. But losses have steadily increased -- the main reasons given by politicians are a lack of skilled staff, ageing infrastructure, a lack of information, and tariffs not reflecting the full costs of delivering water. The situation is the same across the country. A report by the Water Research Commission two years ago found that on average a third -- roughly 37% of water was lost in municipalities. This was either from leaks, or from people not paying for their water – both are included in "non-revenue water". So how has the situation changed in the last two years?
metadata.Further information: To take a current snapshot of the problem of drought and broken infrastructure, we fly to some of the worst drought affected parts of the country and see the state of broken, leaking infrastructure that has caused inconvenience, expense and increasingly threatens health. Gauteng, with its growing population and industry, faces the biggest crunch in the future. It is already using 98% of its allocated water, and relies on Lesotho for a big chunk of the water sitting in the Vaal Dam. The next stage of the Lesotho Highlands Water Scheme only comes online in 2020, and the province will be running on the edge until then. So we feature the case of Martha Mokate — Meadowlands — an active member of the Soweto Electricity Crisis Committee and Gauteng Water Caucus, Martha plays a strong role in the community and has been fighting for remediation and reparation of the situation in Meadowlands for at least the last ten years. In the Gauteng Water Caucus, they expose the ineffectiveness of municipalities in rectifying infrastructure problems amongst other problems. Martha & neighbours’ houses are regularly flooded (and have been for the last 10 years…they’ve lived there in houses they inherited from their parents in the 1950s) because there are no storm water drains and the pipes that municipal workers come to fix, regularly spring leaks again. Their children’s eyes are affected by the dust from the mine dumps behind their houses. That dust infects their lungs and, in the rainy season, the acid, toxic water flows off those dumps into their houses together with sewage from the overloaded sewer system. We also look at Villiers/Qalabotja where Pieter vd Westhuizen says an already dire situation with run-down infrastructure has become worse due to drought, which is very visible and severe there — at a meeting of the Committee on MONDAY this week, it was decided to initiate a pro-active action plan, due to the reigning drought conditions, to approach the authorities to help with an increase in suspected water-related health problems probably caused by the very low water levels of the Vaal which is causing an existing water system contaminated by spillages of raw sewage to become more concentrated. They’re asking for an increase in the water flow from the Grootdraai Dam (the transfer scheme that brings water from Lesotho, through the Drakensberg Rain Factory, to the Vaal system)...as this will definitely contribute to a positive effect in the water quality. As Villiers and Qalabotjha are constantly facing interruptions in water supply, certain of the communities gather their water needs directly from the Vaal river…and the local Mafube Mun as are in contempt of four High Court Orders (Civil Actions) since 2004 due to water pollution. Mafube Municipality are often found to be unable to fund chemicals to service their water works, which is having a definite effect on the water quality in this region. Directives were issued by DWA against Mafube Mun in the past under more favourable conditions with less than zero effect and it is a known fact that Mafube Mun is unable to make contributions as far as their water levies are concerned We put the narratives from various towns together through the eyes of experts who have watched the national picture for a long time -- Paul Fairall form "National Wetlands in Crisis" and the "Jukskei River Catchment Area Management Forum", as well as Afriforum whose members are in fact some of the retired engineers and technicians that could and should maintain the system. We also speak to the Department of Cooperative Governance about efforts in the "Back to Basics" programme to get infrastructure repaired and working in municipalities where capacity has long been eroded.
